Plan by age · Stage 3 of 5

Ages 55–59: Early-exit options

In the late 50s the rules on reaching your own money loosen: the rule of 55 for workplace plans, then 59½ for IRAs. That makes an earlier exit possible, sometimes by choice and sometimes because of a layoff or buyout.

It is also when the question of where you will live gets real: staying, downsizing, moving to another state, or retiring abroad. Each choice changes taxes, healthcare and how far the money goes.

  2. 50–54The catch-up years
  3. 55–59Early-exit options

Birthdays that matter

  • 55HSA catch-up: you can add $1,000 a year once you are 55. IRS Publication 969: HSAs
  • 55Rule of 55: leave an employer in or after the year you turn 55 and withdrawals from that employer's plan avoid the 10% additional tax. IRS: Exceptions to tax on early distributions
  • 59½IRA and plan withdrawals no longer face the 10% additional tax. IRS: Significant ages for retirement plan participants

Life events in this stage

  1. Early access rules: 55 and 59½
  2. Job loss, buyout or forced early retirement
  3. Pension or lump sum choices
  4. Downsizing or relocating, including abroad

Early access rules: 55 and 59½

What's happening

Before 59½, most retirement withdrawals carry a 10% additional tax on top of income tax. The rule of 55 is an exception for the workplace plan of the employer you leave in or after the year you turn 55. It does not apply to IRAs.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Which account funds which years, from your last paycheck to Social Security.
  • Keeping money in the employer plan versus rolling it to an IRA.

Common mistakes

  • Rolling a 401(k) into an IRA at 55 and then needing the money before 59½.
  • Assuming the rule of 55 covers every old employer plan; it covers the plan of the job you leave at 55 or later.

Key numbers for 2026

  • age 55Rule of 55Separation from service in or after the year you turn 55 (50 for some public safety workers).Source: IRS: Exceptions to tax on early distributions
  • 59½Penalty-free withdrawalsThe 10% additional tax on early distributions stops applying at 59½.Source: IRS: Significant ages for retirement plan participants
  • $1,000HSA catch-upExtra yearly HSA contribution from age 55.Source: IRS Publication 969: HSAs

Job loss, buyout or forced early retirement

What's happening

Layoffs and buyouts often land in the late 50s, sometimes years before the date in your plan. The first 60 days matter most: health coverage, severance terms and whether to touch retirement money.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Look for the next job, consult or retire now.
  • Whether a low-income year is a chance for a Roth conversion.

Common mistakes

  • Letting health coverage lapse while deciding.
  • Taking a check from the 401(k) instead of a direct rollover, which triggers 20% withholding.

Key numbers for 2026

  • generally 18 monthsCOBRA continuationAfter a job loss or cut in hours; some events allow up to 36 months.Source: U.S. Department of Labor: COBRA FAQs
  • 60 daysSpecial Enrollment PeriodLosing job-based coverage lets you buy a Marketplace plan within 60 days.Source: HealthCare.gov: Special Enrollment Periods
  • 20%Withholding on indirect rolloversPlans must withhold 20% if they pay you instead of rolling over directly.Source: IRS: Rollovers of retirement plan and IRA distributions

Pension or lump sum choices

What's happening

If you have a pension, your employer may offer a monthly payment for life or a one-time lump sum. Some people consider buying an annuity with savings. These choices are usually permanent.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Guaranteed income versus control of a lump sum.
  • Single-life versus joint-and-survivor payments.

Common mistakes

  • Comparing a lump sum to the monthly payment without counting how long you and a spouse might live.
  • Buying an annuity you do not fully understand from a salesperson paid by commission.

Key numbers for 2026

  • 20%Withholding on indirect rolloversA lump sum paid to you, not rolled over directly, has 20% withheld.Source: IRS: Rollovers of retirement plan and IRA distributions

Downsizing or relocating, including abroad

What's happening

Where you live sets your largest costs: housing, state taxes and healthcare. Some people downsize to free up home equity, some move to a lower-cost state, and some retire abroad.

What to do now

Key decisions

  • Downsize, move to another state, move abroad or stay.
  • Buy or rent in the new place.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a cheaper place is cheaper once healthcare, travel home and taxes are counted.
  • Dropping Medicare Part B when moving abroad without knowing the late-enrollment penalty if you come back.

Key numbers for 2026

  • $250,000 / $500,000Home sale exclusionGain excluded if you owned and lived in the home 2 of the last 5 years (single / married filing jointly).Source: IRS Topic 701: Sale of your home
  • generally not coveredMedicare outside the U.S.Medicare pays for care abroad only in rare cases.Source: Medicare.gov: Travel outside the U.S.
